Six-Mode MZI-Based Post-Selected CZ Gate: Fabrication-Error Simulator

Exact two-photon model (permanents of U6), |++⟩ metrics. Ideal gate: F = 1, P = 1/9 = 0.1111. A software model for design studies: no hardware data, and COMSOL validation is planned.

New here? Start with this

What is this? A light-based quantum gate (a controlled-Z gate) is built from three small interferometers (MZIs) on a chip. Real chips are never exactly as designed: the gap between two waveguides can be a few nanometres off, which changes how light is shared. This page shows how much such errors hurt the gate and how much the on-chip heaters can fix.

F: conditional fidelity
How close the gate's output is to the ideal one, given that the gate worked. 1.000 is perfect. Below about 0.99 the gate is noticeably wrong.
P: success probability
How often the gate works at all. The ideal design succeeds 1 time in 9 (0.1111). The gate is post-selected, not heralded: you only know it worked when both photons arrive in the right output pair, and that detection uses them up.
ε: coupler error
How far a 50:50 coupler is from 50:50. A coupler passes a fraction T = 0.5 + ε of the light straight through. ε = +0.04 means 54:46.

Three steps

  1. Press Next ▶ in the guided demo (box 1) to follow the story: ideal gate, paper case, heater repair.
  2. Move the sliders in boxes 2 to 4 (nanometre errors, per-coupler errors, phase errors). Watch F and P in Gate performance; the sentence under them says in plain words what the numbers mean.
  3. Use box 5 to let the heaters re-tune the phases, and box 6 to see how many random chips would still work.

Heaters change the optical phase of a waveguide by warming it. "Recalibration" means finding new heater settings that cancel the effect of the fixed coupler errors.

1 · Guided demo

2 · Manufacturing errors (nm) → coupler error ε

In plain words: if the waveguide gap, width or the wavelength is slightly off, every coupler splits light slightly unevenly. These sliders convert nanometres into that splitting error ε using a mode-solver model.
Surrogate EM model: semi-vectorial solver, 450×220 nm Si, 200 nm gap, 1550 nm. Not a COMSOL result.
Cross-check status. An independent full-vector solver (femwell) agrees on the coupling strength within about 4% and on the gap sensitivity within 1%, so "6 nm of gap error → ε ≈ +0.04" holds. It disagrees on the width sensitivity by about 18% (−9.67 vs −8.21 per µm). Tick the box to use the full-vector value; every width-dependent number on this page, including the yield, then changes. COMSOL validation is planned.

3 · Extra error per coupler (T = 0.5 + εproc + εi)

In plain words: each of the six couplers can also be off by its own amount, on top of the common error from box 2.
Reading "Paper case": +0.04 is an absolute shift of the power transmission T of each 50:50 coupler, from 0.50 to 0.54. That is +4 percentage points, or +8% relative to 0.5. It is not "±4% on the 1/3 splitting ratio": that reduced model gives F ≥ 0.997 only. The effective 1/3 splitting comes from the MZI phase α. With the EM model of box 2, +0.04 corresponds to a common gap error of about 6 nm.

4 · Uncontrolled phase errors (degrees)

In plain words: unwanted phase shifts (path-length changes, heater drift) that the controller does not know about.
Couplers are designed 50:50 inside each MZI. The effective 1/3 splitting is set by the MZI phase α. ε is an absolute power error. These sliders move the model coordinates α and β. A drift in one physical heater also shifts the whole MZI's phase, which acts as a small single-qubit error, so per heater the sensitivity is a little higher (about 4.5 instead of 4.25 for the centre MZI).

5 · Fix it with the heaters (phase recalibration)

In plain words: the heaters cannot repair the couplers, but they can re-tune the interference so the gate output is correct again. The paper retunes three phases (α only); retuning all six can recover the gate completely, within the reach limit below.
α only is the paper's recalibration: the three splitting phases, with P kept at or above 1/9 (the best α setting meets that anyway). It gains almost nothing in F (0.9871 → 0.9875) because, at T = 0.54, most of the damage is a 12.9° phase on |11⟩, and α cannot correct a phase. Retuning just the two β phases already gives F = 0.9997. The larger P (0.1119 → 0.1177) is not a recovery, because the ideal P is 0.1111. All six phases (five matter, since β_A only acts on an empty mode) recover F = 1.0000 and P = 1/9 for the paper case.

Splitting reach per MZI

Reach is a necessary condition: the MZI must be able to split at 2/3. For equal couplers the limit is |ε| ≤ 1/(2√3) ≈ 0.289. Strongly unequal couplers can leave a small residual even when reachable, so always read F.

6 · How many chips would work? (Monte Carlo yield)

In plain words: make many virtual chips with random errors and count how many still reach F ≥ 0.99, with and without heater tuning. Only 120 chips by default, so results move by about ±0.003 between runs.

7 · Which phase shifter? (heater or electro-optic)

In plain words: the phases above are set by phase shifters. Heaters add no loss but are slow; silicon electro-optic shifters are fast but their charge carriers absorb photons, which lowers P and can unbalance the gate. Values after re-tuning all nine drives.

Heaters: Pπ ≈ 19 mW each, about 175 mW for the whole gate. Full details, plots and assumptions: Chip & EM views ▸ Phase shifters tab. Silicon EO numbers use the Soref–Bennett model with core-only doping, so they are optimistic.

What this simulator does, and what it does not

  • Does: exact six-mode, two-photon model of the gate (permanents of the 6×6 transfer matrix); coupler errors from a semi-vectorial finite-difference mode solver; heater recalibration; Monte Carlo yield.
  • Also: a phase-shifter comparison (heaters versus electro-optic shifters, box 7 and the Phase shifters tab).
  • Checked: F and P agree with the independent Python model; closed-form amplitudes agree to 10-16. The mode solver was cross-checked against a full-vector solver (femwell): coupling strength within about 4%, gap sensitivity within 1%, width sensitivity about 18% different (see box 2). Absolute effective indices from the finite-difference solver are about 2% high.
  • Does not: use any hardware measurement; model heater crosstalk, photon distinguishability, detector dark counts, sidewall angle or roughness here (simplified studies of crosstalk and distinguishability are on the Chip & EM page and are design trends, not predictions); treat the swap network of larger cascades.
  • Status: pre-COMSOL estimates. COMSOL validation is planned; nothing here replaces it.
